results.title: A comparison of nonparametric and parametric methods to adjust for baseline measures - ScienceDirect
results.content: # A comparison of nonparametric and parametric methods to adjust for baseline measures. When analyzing the randomized controlled trial, we may employ various statistical methods to adjust for baseline measures. Depending on the method chosen to adjust for baseline measures, inferential results can vary. We investigate the Type 1 error and statistical power of tests comparing treatment outcomes based on parametric and nonparametic methods. For randomized controlled trials, inferential results may vary depending on whether or not an individual subject's baseline data are adjusted for, as well as the method chosen to adjust. Either the post-treatment value or change from baseline may be analyzed to account for the effect of the baseline measures. Alternatively, the percent change from baseline, a scale invariant method can also be used. Lord's paradox states that the relationship between a continuous outcome and a categorical exposure may be reversed when an additional continuous covariate (e.g., baseline measures) is introduced [1]. Thus, appropriate inferential procedures must be employed to adjust for baseline measures. Previously, Vickers [2] has compared several parametric *t*-test and ANCOVA based methods in a large sample setting. He recommended the use of ANCOVA which had the greatest power in the case of normally-distributed data, when baseline and post-baseline data are correlated. In Section 2, we review commonly-used nonparametric methods and parametric univariate methods to compare change scores and percent change from baseline. We also compare different multivariate regression methods to adjust for the baseline. To compare the Type 1 errors and powers (i.e., 1-Type 2 errors) of seven methods (e.g., hypothesis tests or regression-based comparisons), we generate random samples with 1000 repetitions of the active and control (say, *A* vs. We illustrate the nonparametric and parametric methods investigated via simulations on two published examples, i.e., a product assay and dental caries example, found in the statistical literature. Such methods should be pre-specified in the statistical analysis plan prior to conducting a prospective clinical trial. ### Stat Med. ### The use of percentage change from baseline as an outcome in a controlled trial is statistically inefficient: a simulation study. ### Modern robust statistical methods: an easy way to maximize the accuracy and power of your research.

Wolters Kluwer full text link. # Pulsed Field Ablation Versus High-Power Short-Duration Ablation in Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic and Meta-Analysis. # Pulsed Field Ablation Versus High-Power Short-Duration Ablation in Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic and Meta-Analysis. ### Authors. To compare the efficacy, safety, and procedural characteristics of pulsed field ablation (PFA) versus high-power short-duration (HPSD) radiofrequency ablation in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and observational studies comparing PFA and HPSD in AF ablation. A comprehensive search was performed in PubMed and relevant databases through July 2025. A total of 12 studies were included, with data extracted on baseline characteristics, procedural details, clinical outcomes, and complications. Risk of bias was assessed using appropriate tools for randomized and nonrandomized studies. Statistical pooling was conducted using random-effects models where feasible. Across 12 studies including over 2000 patients, freedom from AF at 12 months was similar between PFA (mean 85.3%) and HPSD (mean 83.2%). PFA demonstrated a lower incidence of complications such as cardiac tamponade, phrenic nerve injury, and esophageal damage. Procedural parameters such as fluoroscopy time, energy delivery, and touch-up requirements favored PFA in multiple studies. PFA offers comparable efficacy to HPSD while demonstrating a superior safety profile and procedural efficiency, supporting its role as a favorable ablation modality for AF. atrial fibrillation; catheter ablation techniques; high-power short-duration ablation; pulmonary vein isolation; pulsed field ablation. results.title: Evaluating Pre-training Datasets
results.content: Better dataset evaluation => Robust datasets => Powerful models. Capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) hinges heavily on the quality and quantity of the data they are trained on. LLM training dataset collection and curation takes massive amounts of spend and compute. This brings us to the crucial question: how do we ensure the quality of massive, datasets used for pretraining these powerful models? The post**_FineWeb: A Deep Dive into Open Datasets for Large Language Model Pretraining_**offers a practical framework. 1. **The Challenge of Dataset Evaluation**. Evaluating datasets for LLM pretraining is a complex task. Traditional metrics often fall short of capturing the nuances of linguistic quality, factual accuracy, and overall alignment with human language use required for effective LLM training. Moreover, directly evaluating a massive dataset by training a full-scale LLM on it is computationally prohibitive and impractical ~ O(millions of $ spend). Smaller model based dataset evaluation:**. Here’s a blueprint for a granular and cost-effective analysis of the dataset’s impact on model performance. 1. **Dataset candidate generation:** Create different variants of the dataset by varying factors like size (number of examples), filtering criteria (duplication, language, low quality text etc), and data augmentation techniques. 2. **Proxy Training with Smaller Models (Ablation models):** Instead of directly training massive or target LLM (xx B parameter), leverage smaller models (125M — 2B parameter models) as proxies to evaluate the dataset’s impact on performance. Train these smaller models on all dataset candidates. 3. **Comprehensive Benchmark Evaluation:** Evaluate the trained models on a diverse set of standard benchmarks that cover a wide range of language understanding and generation capabilities. 4. **Correlation Analysis:** Analyze the correlation between dataset characteristics and model performance on the benchmarks to identify the most crucial factors for dataset quality. * **Small variance between runs** trained on different variations of the same dataset. * Performance above random baseline for this task by at least a few standard deviations: given the smaller ablation models and trainings make sure that the scores are **above random noise**. The methodology of using smaller ablation models is not just about evaluating existing datasets; it’s about informing the creation of better datasets in the future. Title: Beginner’s Guide to Trustworthy A/B Tests i.e. Controlled Experiments | by Yash Gupta | Medium
# Beginner’s Guide to Trustworthy A/B Tests i.e. Controlled Experiments. A/B testing is essentially an experiment where two or more variants of a page are shown to users at random, and statistical analysis is used to determine which variation performs better for a given conversion goal. * Sample Size Calculation aka Statistical Power Analysis. **Variant:** A user experience being tested by changing certain parameters/inputs. A/B tests generally have 2 variants — Control and Treatment. **Randomisation Unit:** Units (users/pages/sessions/user-day) are randomly assigned to the variants to ensure that the populations assigned to different variants are statistically similar, allowing causal effects to be determined with high probability. * The sensitivity or ability to detect statistically significant differences improves with Lower variance in the estimate i.e. lower the std error in the mean of the metric. * Understanding the variability of estimates of the metric will help us size the experiment properly and while conducting statistical significance analysis. *The probability of committing a type I error (rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true) is called α (alpha) the other name for this is the level of statistical significance.*. Statistical significance refers to the claim that a result from data generated by testing or experimentation is likely to be attributable to a specific cause. Statistical Power is the probability of detecting a significant difference between the variants when there INDEED IS A DIFFERENCE. The quantity (1 — β) is called power, the probability of observing an effect in the sample (if one), of a specified effect size or greater exists in the population.*. ## Sample Size Calculation aka Statistical Power Analysis. * A Power analysis helps in determining the sample size for running the experiment to ensure we don’t underpower the experiment. * Bernoiulli metric Sample size Calculation using Power analysis —. ## Default values for Statistical Significance, Power and Recommendations Rationale:. Data for the experiment and control group metrics can be fed into one of the following online statistical analysis tools or MS Excel to check for statistical significance:. ## A/B Testing Calculator for Statistical Significance | SurveyMonkey. We can actually use sophisticated methods that leverage pre-experiment data to reduce our variance, thus shrinking our confidence intervals and speeding up tests.

results.title: Is it time to rethink pre-post randomised controlled trials in strength and conditioning? : A review of statistical approaches with derivations and simulations. | SportRxiv
results.content: # Is it time to rethink pre-post randomised controlled trials in strength and conditioning? Statistics, RCT, Statistical power, sample size, measurement error. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) featuring a single measurement at baseline and post-intervention is the most common study type used to build an evidence base in strength and conditioning. Realistic pre-post RCT data were simulated for strength and conditioning interventions based on parameters obtained from recent large meta-analyses. A total of nine outcomes from three domains (strength, power, and speed) were simulated whilst adjusting for a range of factors including sample size (N=10,15,25, and 50), the average treatment effect (ATE), the relationship between baseline and change scores, the amount of baseline imbalance, and measurement error. In the worst-case scenario (e.g., N=10, small ATE and large measurement error) statistical power was likely to be ~0.1. Even with sample sizes of 50, statistical power was unlikely to exceed 0.4 when combined with small ATE and large measurement error. The results of this study show that sample sizes and ATE commonly investigated in strength and conditioning are likely to lead to a high proportion of inferential errors. traditional resistance training methods on adaptations in strength, power, and sprint speed: A systematic review, meta-analysis, and quality of evidence appraisal.
